summary: Asks the network community for comments on how socket names should be structured. Two layouts are offered for the 32-bit socket number, one almost entirely arbitrary and one with defined fields. It answers a request made at the February 1971 meeting in Illinois.

plainLanguage.summary: A socket number is like a mailbox address. This note shows two ways to build that address and asks everyone which they prefer.

questions: how should socket numbers be structured
what socket name layouts were proposed in 1971
subtitle: Two layouts for 32-bit socket names and four schemes for handing them out, offered for comment in 1971.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the early network needed a way to name sockets so that two users could find each other and be confident they were talking to the right party.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents two socket name structures, an arbitrary 31-bit number or a 24-bit user ID plus a 7-bit tag, each ending in a gender bit, and weighs four assignment schemes.
tldr.outcome: It makes no final decision. It asks readers to respond through the standard RFC mechanism, and the unit metadata shows it was updated by RFC 147.

today: RFC 129 is a request for comments rather than a specification; it was updated by RFC 147.

sections.title: Two Socket Name Structures
sections.content:
The RFC answers a request, made at the February NWG meeting at the University of Illinois, for comments on suggested socket name structures. Both structures are 32 bits and end in a one-bit gender.

  • Structure 1: 31 bits of arbitrary value, then the gender bit.
  • Structure 2: a 24-bit user ID, a 7-bit tag, then the gender bit. This ties sockets to users rather than processes.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a mailbox number made of digits. One way lets you pick any digits you like. The other way starts the number with your own ID.

sections.title: Schemes One to Three
sections.content:
The example is User A at Host A connecting to User B at Host B at an agreed time, and the issues are addressing and security.

Scheme 1 lets users pick any 32-bit identifier, with the least significant bit as gender (0 read, 1 write) and only one active socket per identifier at a host. It is simple and reasonably safe in a non-malicious environment, but conflicts are possible and each pair needs a prior confidential exchange.

Scheme 2 has the host choose the identifier, with a Network Directory service relating identifiers to user names. It allows symbolic addressing but is cumbersome and not absolutely secure, since a socket can be deactivated and its name reused.

Scheme 3 uses administratively assigned user identifiers, which gives each user a selection of 256 sockets. It prevents naming conflicts and allows open arrangements, but some systems may be unable to ensure user ID integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: You can pick your own mailbox number, ask the post office to hand you one and look it up in a phone book, or get a number that starts with your own personal code. Each way has good and bad points.

sections.title: Scheme Four: Naming Programs
sections.content:
Scheme 4 argues that connections are between programs, so programs rather than users should be identified. A program has a fixed, unique identifier plus a range of variable identifiers, one per connection. User IDs can be sent after a service is requested.

As an example, Rand's Network Services Program uses a 24-bit administratively assigned program number, a 7-bit multiplex code and a gender bit. Structure 1 can accommodate this and other schemes layered on its arbitrary field.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the mailbox number says which program owns it, plus a small extra number for each separate conversation.

fields.name: Tag
fields.desc: Distinguishes sockets of the same user.
